segments.title: Opening: The Fog That Chokes England

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, careful, and occasionally delighted journey through one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be reading Dickens's monumental novel passage by passage — the fog, the courts, the characters who haunt you long after the last page.
Three brilliant readers join me today, and I want to introduce them properly, because each brings something the novel genuinely needs.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score, in rhythm and performance and comic timing.
If anyone can tell us what Dickens wrote for the voice rather than the page, it's Oliver.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian whose speciality is the institutions that Victorian literature puts on trial.
When Dickens puts the Court of Chancery in the dock, James will tell us exactly what was really happening there — and why it mattered so much.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered — which is, I think, the correct response.
She brings the reader's eye — the eye that catches the verbal music, the sentence you have to read twice, the character who deserves far better than they get.
We begin today with atmosphere — the way Dickens builds a world through space, through rooms, through the physical fabric of things.
Oliver, you've spent a professional lifetime inhabiting fictional spaces through your voice — shall we start with Bleak House itself?
Gladly — and I should say that Bleak House the building presents a narrator's first beautiful problem, which is that it isn't bleak at all.
Esther arrives expecting something grim and finds something almost absurdly warm and hospitable and peculiar.

The furnishings alone are a complete comic world — portraits split across rooms, a trout staring at paintings of China tea ceremonies, four angels of Queen Anne's reign hauling a complacent gentleman to heaven.
Dickens is doing something sly here: the house is named for despair but furnished for delight.
And then Esther — our reliable, understated Esther — delivers the summation, and it is one of the loveliest compound sentences in the book.

"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House"
That phrase — "a low accompaniment to everything we heard" — that's a novelist thinking like a composer.
He's scoring the scene.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is the strangeness Dickens allows to coexist with the warmth.
The house is hospitable and also quite odd — birds in frames staring at a real trout, portraits whose relatives have been separated across different rooms.
It's as if Jarndyce has assembled the world's most eccentric comfort deliberately — and perhaps he has.
There's a sentence I always stop at: "They agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the whitest linen."

"They agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of rose-leaves and sweet lavender."
Rose-leaves and sweet lavender in every drawer.
That is a very specific kind of love — someone has prepared this place for other people's comfort with extraordinary care.
It tells you everything about Jarndyce before Dickens says a word about his character directly.
The warmth of that domestic space is not incidental — it is, I think, structurally necessary to what Dickens is doing.
Bleak House the building is a refuge precisely because the world outside — Chancery, the law, the fog — is actively hostile to human happiness.
And the novel is quite explicit about what that external world does to people — and to the bonds between them.
There is a passage where Gridley's dying words echo through Esther's account of Richard's departure, and they land with terrible force.
"Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for.
There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!"
"The only tie Chancery has not broken."
That is the institutional violence this novel is documenting — not dramatic, not sudden, but slow, grinding, and total.
James is right, and I think the genius of the novel is that Dickens shows you the warm rooms first.
He makes you love the refuge before he shows you how thoroughly the outside world can destroy everything.
But the novel also has a counter-example of a domestic interior — and it is one of the funniest, most perfectly observed rooms in all fiction.
Skimpole's sitting room.
The description is almost a moral portrait — the room tells you everything about a man who takes everything and provides nothing.
Dickens gives us the inventory as if he can barely keep the straight face required:

"It was dingy enough and not at all clean, but furnished with an odd kind of shabby luxury, with a large footstool, a sofa, and plenty of cushions, an easy-chair, and plenty of pillows, a piano, books, drawing materials, music, newspapers, and a few sketches and pictures."
And then — because Dickens cannot resist — there is also a broken pane of glass papered over, alongside a little plate of hothouse nectarines.
Nectarines.
The contrast with Bleak House is devastating, isn't it — because Jarndyce's rooms are odd but lovingly cared for, and Skimpole's are luxurious but entirely unlovable.
The footprints on the stairs — dirty footprints, which are the only furnishing visible on the way up — that's an extraordinary detail.
The world tracks through Skimpole's house but nobody cleans it.
And he is reclining on the sofa in his dressing-gown at midday, drinking coffee from old china, looking at wallflowers on the balcony.
It is a portrait of pure, cheerful, irresponsible consumption — and Dickens doesn't editorialize.
He just shows you the room and lets you arrive at the conclusion yourself.
The physical space in this novel is never merely decorative — it is always diagnostic.
Jarndyce's house speaks of responsible care; Skimpole's speaks of a man who has externalized all obligation onto the nearest available person.
And both of those spaces exist in a larger world that the law has made radically unstable.
Gridley's cry — the only tie Chancery has not broken — tells us what is truly at stake whenever we see a warm room in this novel.
The warmth is always under threat.
Warmth under threat — that may be as good a three-word description of this novel as we're likely to find.
In our next segment, we turn to the characters themselves — the living, the dying, and the endlessly, magnificently strange.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: Jo's Erasure from Society

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been circling the novel's great engine of injustice — Chancery — but today we descend to street level.
We're going to look at Jo — the crossing-sweeper, one of the most devastating figures in all of Dickens.
And we're going to look at what the novel says, quite systematically, about the invisible lives of the poor.
With me today: Oliver Trevelyan, actor and audiobook narrator, who hears every word of this novel as performance.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who knows exactly what the institutions in this novel actually did to real people.
And Caroline Woodcourt, critic and devoted re-reader, who never lets the verbal music go unnoticed.
Let's begin with the inquest scene in Chapter Eleven — Jo gives testimony, and the novel does something quite extraordinary with that.
The inquest scene is one of those passages where you can feel Dickens absolutely relishing the performance problem he's set himself.
You have Mrs. Piper giving testimony — and that is a feat of comic writing of the very highest order.
The narrator tells us she has, quote — and I must read this —
"a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
That is Dickens describing Mrs. Piper's speech while simultaneously performing it on the page.
The parentheses breed, the sentences never close — it enacts the very chaos it describes.
And then — after all that glorious noise — Jo steps forward and says almost nothing.
The contrast is devastating.
That contrast is precisely what undoes me every time I read it.
Jo's testimony is rendered in this extraordinary stripped-back style — short declaratives, barely any verbs.
Listen to this passage — it reads almost like a bureaucratic form being completed, except each blank is a wound:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Three negatives in four words, and then four words more.
Dickens doesn't ask us to feel sorry for Jo — the sentence structure does it for him.
It's the most economical grief I've ever encountered on a page.
And yet the coroner's court dismisses him.
Jo cannot take the oath because he has no conception of what the oath means — not from moral failure, but from total social abandonment.
The law as Dickens depicts it here is not indifferent to Jo — it is constitutively incapable of seeing him.
And what is so bitter is that the boy understands the moral universe perfectly well on his own terms.
The passage tells us he knows a broom's a broom and knows it's wicked to tell a lie —
"Don't recollect who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both."
He has absorbed moral knowledge from somewhere — from the air, from the world's indifferent friction against him — and yet that knowledge counts for nothing in a court of law.
What I keep coming back to is the dead man — Nemo — and his relationship with Jo before the inquest.
Dickens calls Jo a "graceless creature" — and then immediately proceeds to give him the most graceful testimony in the chapter.
The irony is doing tremendous work.
Because what Jo remembers about Nemo is this — and it is one of the most quietly shattering moments in the novel:
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging."
Two men — one already dead, one near it — recognizing each other across the same abyss.
And Dickens doesn't sentimentalize it — the exchange is transactional, the price of a supper, and yet it is the most human act in these chapters.
That connects directly to something Esther observes — and I think it's the passage in the whole novel that most openly becomes a polemic.
She watches two poor women — coarse and shabby, as she describes them — and sees the extraordinary tenderness between them.
And then Esther steps back from the scene and says something almost direct to the reader:
"I think the best side of such people is almost hidden from us. What the poor are to the poor is little known, excepting to themselves and God."
That phrase — "excepting to themselves and God" — breaks the social contract of narrative omniscience.
Esther is confessing the limits of her own seeing — and by extension, ours.
Esther's confession of limited seeing is also Dickens's critique of social reform discourse in his own time.
The philanthropic classes of the 1850s were, by and large, speaking about the poor — not with them, and certainly not imagining inner lives of comparable complexity to their own.
Now, the novel also shows us institutions that speak on behalf of the legal subject while quietly devouring them — and Vholes is the supreme example.
He submits his professional duty as a kind of moral alibi — and Dickens captures it with hideous precision.
Listen to Vholes explaining himself to Esther:
"I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
He is performing transparency while being completely opaque about the fact that his duty serves himself, not his client.
It is the grammar of bureaucratic complicity — and it hasn't dated by a single year.
Vholes is brilliant to read aloud precisely because his speech is constructed to sound reasonable.
The sentences are grammatically correct — impeccably so — and morally catastrophic.
And then — right at the end of that speech — he spots Richard arriving and the mask just... flips.
He's suddenly all warmth and pleasantry — "enjoying the pleasure of some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson" — as if the previous two minutes hadn't happened.
As a performer, that pivot is a gift — and a horror.
The structural horror of this section — Jo, the inquest, Vholes — is that they all circle the same absence.
Nobody is actually responsible for Jo's condition — every institution, every individual, can point elsewhere.
And then there is the Mrs. Rouncewell scene — which I find almost unbearable, but in a completely different register.
She is pleading across the entire gulf of class and reserve that separates her from Lady Dedlock — and she knows it.
She says — and it's a speech of such naked dignity:
"I am so humble in my place and you are by nature so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child."
She is not asking Lady Dedlock to feel her pain — she is acknowledging that the system may prevent it — and asking anyway.
Mrs. Rouncewell's speech is a precise anatomization of deference — and of its cost.
She has spent her entire life in service to this family, and the system of that life means she cannot simply demand or accuse.
She must beg — and she describes the architecture of her own subordination with absolute clarity while doing it.
The passage is devastating because the narrator observes that she "pleads with genuine simplicity" — not strategic simplicity, not performed humility.
She means every word.
What strikes me, listening to all of this, is that the novel refuses to assign the machinery of injustice to any single villain.
Jo is abandoned by a system, not a person. Mrs. Rouncewell is constrained by a structure, not a cruelty.
Vholes is — perhaps the most frightening of all — a machine that has mistaken its own functioning for conscience.
In our next segment, we'll look at Chancery itself — and what Dickens understood about institutions that outlive their original purpose.
Stay with us.

segments.title: A Question of Inheritance: Plotting the Dedlock Revelation

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterpiece seriously — passage by passage, chapter by chapter.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's central engines of suspense — the slow, gothic revelation of Lady Dedlock's secret.
The machinery of plot is ticking beautifully in these chapters, and we have three extraordinary readers here to help us take it apart.

Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive — he hears the prose as performance, and what he hears in Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock I suspect will be quite something.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he knows exactly what a solicitor like Tulkinghorn was, what he could do, and what he represented.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House many times over — she'll be attentive to what the novel does to Esther, and why those scenes are among the most quietly devastating Dickens ever wrote.
Let's begin with Tulkinghorn — perhaps the strangest and most menacing figure in a novel that is not short of menacing figures.
Tulkinghorn arrives the way really frightening people do — without hurrying.
Dickens gives us this gorgeous line about his pace — it is never quickened, never slackened.
"He comes towards them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never slackened."
That repetition — never quickened, never slackened — is Dickens writing for the voice.
It's a stage direction as much as a description.
And then we get the real masterstroke — the body as archive.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every crease of his dress — not his mind, not his memory, his dress.
And that image is historically precise, not merely poetic.
Solicitors of the Victorian era who served great families were repositories in the most literal sense — keepers of deeds, wills, correspondence, the paper skeleton of aristocratic life.
Dickens then puts this wonderfully precise qualifier on it.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
He keeps the secrets of others, but his own interiority — his motives, his loyalties — is equally sealed.
The power of a man like Tulkinghorn is precisely that no one knows whether he serves the family or serves himself.
In Victorian legal practice, that ambiguity was the solicitor's greatest professional asset.
What strikes me most is the phrase "he is his own client in that matter."
It's a legal formulation applied to the self — and it makes him frightening in a very modern way.
He has professionalised his own opacity.
And that sets the terms for every encounter he has with Lady Dedlock — two people each concealing something, each watching.
And the watching is relentless — Dickens describes it at extraordinary length in the chapter twelve passages.
Oliver, you've read these scenes aloud — what does the mutual surveillance feel like when you're performing it?
It feels like chess played at absolute stillness.
Dickens tells us Sir Leicester is just — staring at the fire, utterly unaware.
He renews what Dickens calls his stately protest — the Dedlock dignity on autopilot.
And while that dignified obliviousness plays out, these two are locked in.
Listen to how Dickens renders it — he doesn't dramatise it, he annotates it.
"During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another."
Without any other alteration in their customary deportment — that's the whole of it, isn't it.
The terror is invisible to everyone in the room.
And Dickens pushes that further when the scenes extend across subsequent days.
The passage in chapter twelve describing their repeated meetings at Chesney Wold is one of his great exercises in sustained irony.
He describes Lady Dedlock as an exhausted deity — and the phrase deserves a moment.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
The aristocratic performance is a kind of secular religion, and she has to maintain it under existential pressure.
For those who know the secret, the phrase "presiding at her own shrine" takes on a crueller edge — she is performing an identity that may be about to collapse.
And opposite her, Tulkinghorn is described with equal precision — the same speechless repository of noble confidences.
Dickens says he is so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.
That paradox is the key to him — he belongs everywhere among the powerful because power needs people like him.
And then comes the passage I find most haunting in these chapters — the great rolling sentence that closes the whole thing.

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
For the time — that qualifier is doing enormous work.
It tells us this equilibrium is temporary, that revelation is coming, and that the novel has already decided the outcome — we just don't know when.
That sentence is a gift to read aloud.
The triple anaphora — whether each, whether each, what each — has a kind of judicial rhythm, like a summing up.
And James's point about the aristocratic performance under pressure — I think that's what makes Lady Dedlock so difficult to play.
You can never let the mask slip — not yet — but the reader has to feel the effort it costs her to keep it on.
Let's turn now to the other half of this revelation — not the one being watched, but the one who watches without knowing what she's seeing.
Esther Summerson meets Lady Dedlock in chapter eighteen — and what happens to her is one of the strangest and most moving moments in the entire novel.
Caroline, this is your territory.
This scene undoes me every time.
Esther is in the room with Lady Dedlock — a woman she has never met — and she stands up and meets her eyes.
And Dickens describes what happens with this extraordinary double question — it's Esther's voice, looking back.

"Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the look I met as I stood up! Shall I ever forget the manner in which those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and to hold mine!"
Spring out of their languor — that verb is perfect.
Lady Dedlock is always performing exhaustion and boredom — and in this one instant, something real breaks through.
And only Esther sees it, because only Esther could understand what it means — except she doesn't yet.
The rhetorical questions are doing something very unusual there.
Esther is narrating retrospectively — she already knows who Lady Dedlock is, she knows the whole tragedy.
So "Shall I ever forget" carries an unbearable irony — no, she never will, and we know why.
It's among the cleverest double-time narration in the whole novel.
And what follows in the next passage deepens the strangeness considerably.
Esther can't account for what she feels — she's certain she has never seen this woman before.
And yet something is awakened in her that goes all the way back to childhood.

"And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."
The detail of standing on tiptoe to reach the glass — that is not sentiment, that is psychological precision.
The body remembering before the mind can articulate what it remembers.
And Esther tries to reason it away — she considers whether Lady Dedlock resembles her godmother.
She rejects it — the expression is quite different, the severity is absent.
But she can't quite escape the sense of being summoned.

"And yet I—I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady."
That repetition of the first person — I, I — is Dickens giving Esther a stammer of self-recognition.
And on whose birthday there was no rejoicing — it's the loneliest parenthesis in the novel.
The child who didn't know she had a mother has just looked into her mother's eyes.
And the devastating thing is that both of them know something has happened — and neither of them can say it.
Lady Dedlock's eyes spring out of their languor — that's not the bored aristocrat.
That's recognition, and terror, and love all arriving simultaneously and having to be instantly suppressed.
And Esther goes back to her book — released again, she says, as if she's only been held for a moment.
But she hasn't been released at all.
What I find remarkable, drawing these passages together, is how Dickens handles three different kinds of concealment simultaneously.
Tulkinghorn concealing his motives from everyone including us, Lady Dedlock concealing her past with enormous effort, and Esther concealing nothing — but being concealed from herself.
The plot is all about what people know and what they cannot yet afford to say.
We'll be continuing next time to follow where this slow-burning revelation leads — and it leads somewhere truly shattering.
Thank you to Oliver Trevelyan, Professor James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt.
Bleak House Unpacked — we'll see you in the next chapter.

segments.title: Richard's Slide: Ambition Consumed by the Law

utterances.text: We turn now to one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs: the destruction of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as everything a young man should be — charming, warm, full of possibility.
And then Chancery gets hold of him.
Caroline, you've called this one of the great slow tragedies in the English novel — what makes it land so hard?
What gets me is how early the warning signs are visible — and how Richard himself can almost articulate the problem.
There's this extraordinary moment in chapter seventeen where Esther presses him, gently, about his future with Ada.
And Richard doesn't deflect or make excuses — he confesses, with real candour, to something he can barely name.
He calls Esther 'Mother Hubbard,' which is very Richard — he can't even begin a serious speech without a joke to soften it.
But then listen to what he actually says:

"I seem to want something or other to stand by. Even you have no idea how fond I am of Ada (my darling cousin, I love you, so much!), but I don't settle down to constancy in other things. It's such uphill work, and it takes such a time!"
That parenthetical — 'my darling cousin, I love you, so much!' — it's almost unbearable.
He genuinely loves Ada. That is never in doubt. And he still cannot hold himself together.
The parenthetical is doing so much work there — it's the cry of a young man who knows he's being found out and can only answer with sincerity.
As a performer, I'd play that line very fast, very private — almost as though he's turned away from Esther to say it.
'It's such uphill work, and it takes such a time!' — that's not self-pity, it's bafflement.
He doesn't understand why he can't be the man he wants to be. That's the tragedy before the tragedy.
And then of course he finds his answer — or thinks he does. He'll study law. He'll be in Kenge's office.
He'll have, as he puts it — and the 'hum!' in the middle of the sentence is just perfect Dickens —
"my eye on the—hum!—the forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it."
He thinks he's found the thing to stand by. He's chosen quicksand.
That 'forbidden ground' is revealing in a way Richard doesn't intend.
Chancery in the mid-nineteenth century was genuinely labyrinthine — suits could run for decades, generating fees for lawyers while the principals slowly bled out.
Richard's plan to 'master it' from within a solicitor's office is not merely deluded — it's the precisely wrong response.
The closer you got to Chancery, the more it consumed you. Proximity was not power — it was exposure.
Esther understands this with her instincts, even where she can't quite articulate it as legal critique.
She notes, very quietly, that it was part of Richard's affectionate consideration for Ada —
"not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives."
She frames it as care for Ada. But the warning she is issuing is also a warning about the suit itself.
And Jarndyce watches all of this. That detail Dickens gives us — I find it haunting.
Esther records the precise moment when his expression changes — the first time the shadow falls.
She writes:
"This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with something of a shadow on their benevolent expression."
'Benevolent expression' — that word 'benevolent' has been Jarndyce's defining quality up to this point.
And now it's shadowed. Something has entered it that Esther doesn't name but we feel.
It's grief, partly. But also, I think, foreknowledge. He has seen this before.
Jarndyce is the one character who has survived Chancery with his humanity intact — just barely, but intact.
He knows the mechanism. He has watched it work on others. And now it's aimed at someone he loves.
Which brings us to what Esther sees in chapter twenty-three — and this passage I think is one of the greatest in the whole book.
Richard is now haunting the court. He's friends with Miss Flite. He believes — he genuinely believes — that a favourable judgment is imminent.
And Esther watches him and thinks what no one in the novel will say aloud to him:
"what a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind."
'Riveting.' That word. It's mechanical, it's permanent, it's violent.
Richard is being bolted to Miss Flite's wreckage. And he's laughing while it happens.
The parallelism in that sentence is extraordinary as rhetoric — 'fresh youth' against 'faded age,' 'free hopes' against 'caged birds.'
Miss Flite's birds are not just a symbol — they're a prognosis. They represent what Chancery does to its victims over time.
And Esther sees it. But she also notes something that chills me: 'every one of them sunk him deeper in the infatuation.'
The arguments he reads to reassure himself — each one deepens the delusion rather than testing it.
That is a precise description of how motivated reasoning works. Dickens understood the psychology long before it had a name.
What's extraordinary is that Richard can see himself — briefly, imperfectly — and still cannot stop.
The self-knowledge is there. The will is not.
We'll return to Richard's story — and to Ada's quiet suffering alongside it — as the novel deepens.
But first, we step back to look at the institution that is eating him alive — the Court of Chancery itself.

segments.title: Dickens at Play: Comic Grotesque and Moral Indignation

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the great English novels apart — carefully, lovingly, and without mercy.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the novel's comic and social heart — the place where Dickens is simultaneously the funniest writer in the language and the most furious.
With me today are three readers who know this territory intimately.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than anyone alive, and he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score — every rhythm, every rest.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian whose work on the institutions Dickens depicts is, frankly, essential reading.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has been re-reading this novel since her teens and still finds things that stop her cold.
Today's segment asks a question that sits at the core of Bleak House: how does the same novelist put the Noodle satire and Jo's grief on the same page and make both work?
The Noodle passage is one of the great set pieces in the English comic tradition — full stop.
Dickens is doing something quite specific there: he is showing you that the entire edifice of British government rests not on principle or talent but on social accommodation.
And he makes the absurdity visible through the names alone — Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Goodle, Hoodle — you're laughing before he's even made the argument.
But then comes the sentence that lands the blow.
"What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The parenthesis about Sir Leicester's patriotism — that little blade slipped in mid-sentence — that is Dickens at the absolute height of his craft.
Oliver is right that the comedy is devastating, but I want to underline what Dickens is historically accurate about here.
The early Victorian ministry was genuinely organized around the management of factions and the distribution of patronage to suitable gentlemen.
The offices Dickens lists — Home Department, Exchequer, Colonies, Foreign Office — these were real rewards in a real system of managed loyalty.
What makes Lord Boodle's speech so perfectly observed is the gravity with which he delivers this nonsense.
Dickens tells us he speaks "with much gravity, after dinner" — and that detail, after dinner, places the entire political class in their natural habitat.
These men genuinely perceive the failure to accommodate Noodle as a constitutional crisis.
And the tragedy — which Dickens will make visible through Jo within the same chapters — is that the machinery grinding those boys into the pavement runs on exactly that same indifference.
What strikes me every time I re-read those chapters together is the deliberateness of the juxtaposition.
Because directly against that carnival of Doodles and Noodles, Dickens places Jo at the cemetery gate.
And look at how he describes him.

"With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to the outside of the iron gate. It holds the gate with its hands and looks in between the bars, stands looking in for a little while."
"It." Not "he." The novel's society has stripped him of personhood so thoroughly that even the prose renders him as a thing.
And then he sweeps.
That pronoun — "it" — I've read that passage aloud many times and I still have to steady myself before it.
Because Dickens then gives you the sweeping, and it is one of the most quietly shattering acts of devotion in the whole novel.
Here is the sentence as it stands on the page.
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
Softly. That adverb is doing enormous work — grief made tender and precise.
And earlier, when Jo speaks of Nemo — that is the voice you have to hear under the broom.
It is worth dwelling on what Jo actually says about this man, because the sentiment is expressed in the only register available to him.
The dialect spelling is not comic here — it is documentary.
Dickens writes, and I want to read this exactly as it stands:

"He wos wery good to me," says the boy, wiping his eyes with his wretched sleeve. "Wen I see him a-layin' so stritched out just now, I wished he could have heerd me tell him so. He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
The repetition — "He wos wery good to me, he wos" — is not an accident of uneducated speech.
It is the formal structure of grief in a person who has no other formal structure available.
A eulogy delivered to nobody, in a language the powerful won't deign to understand.
James, that phrase — "the formal structure of grief" — I think that is exactly what Dickens is building in those Jo passages, consciously and with great care.
And what makes it unbearable — in the best sense — is that Jo's grief is more articulate than anything Lord Boodle manages at dinner.
Boodle lists ministries and their suitable incumbents with the full weight of his education and class.
And Jo wipes his eyes with a wretched sleeve and says what he means.
That is the moral arithmetic of this novel, and it is devastating every single time.
The comic and the tragic turning on the same hinge — that, I think, is what separates Dickens from everyone else working in that register.
Oliver, James, Caroline — thank you.
We'll be back shortly to follow these threads further into the novel's darkness and its strange, stubborn light.

segments.title: The Architecture of Secrets: Narrative Technique and Hidden Truth

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We're in the deep architecture of the novel now — the places where Dickens hides his most devastating observations inside form itself.
Today we're looking at how secrets are built into the very structure of the narrative — legal obfuscation, gothic foreboding, and the tender hopes that survive catastrophe.
James, I want to start with you, because there's a passage that I think is one of the great comic performances in English legal satire.
Mr. Kenge's defence of Vholes — and the parliamentary inquiry that follows — how do you read it?
What Dickens is doing here is something quite precise, and it would be easy to miss just how precise because the comedy is so rich.
He's mapping the exact mechanism by which institutional reform is strangled — not through open corruption, but through the invocation of respectability.
Kenge doesn't say the law is good. He doesn't even really defend it.
He simply says that changing it would destroy a class of men like Mr. Vholes — and that is sufficient.
Listen to the actual words Dickens gives him — this is Kenge in full flight:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
It's the apocalyptic scale of it — the face of the earth — for what amounts to protecting one solicitor's income.
And then the parliamentary minutes — that mock blue-book inquiry — is where Dickens really twists the knife.
Question five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine.
That question number alone tells you everything about how Chancery operates in time.
And it proved fatal to the inquiry — for ten years.
I have performed that passage — actually read it on a stage — and the laughter it gets is slightly horrified laughter.
Because you recognise it. Everyone in the audience has sat in front of a bureaucracy that used its own busyness as a defence against scrutiny.
What I love as a performer is the rhythm of that Kenge speech — the repetition: 'Repeal it, my dear sir?'
It's an orator's trick. He circles back, he inflates, he buries the absurdity inside the decorum.
Dickens understood that the way institutions speak is itself a form of violence — one that disguises itself as courtesy.
What strikes me is how the passage about Vholes sits right alongside passages of genuine gothic dread in this novel.
Because the system that Kenge defends with such magnificent pomposity — that same system is slowly killing people.
And then you turn the page and meet passages like the one about Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock watched by the stars.
The tone shifts completely — and it's almost unbearable.
That passage does something I find genuinely unsettling, even after many readings.
The narrator turns suddenly prophetic — proleptic, if you want the technical term — asking about something that hasn't happened yet.
And the image Dickens chooses is the spade and the digger.
"Where are the digger and the spade, this peaceful night, destined to add the last great secret to the many secrets of the Tulkinghorn existence?"
"Is the man born yet, is the spade wrought yet?"
The grave is already implicit in the scene — and Tulkinghorn doesn't know it, but the narrator does, and we do.
That's a very particular kind of dramatic irony — one that implicates the reader in the knowledge of coming death.
James used the word 'secrets' — and it's the word Dickens uses too, that accumulating phrase: the many secrets of the Tulkinghorn existence.
There's a wonderful passage that I'm assigned — George Rouncewell walking through Chesney Wold at night — that picks up exactly this texture of haunted emptiness.
He's holding up his light in a great house. All around him are the traces — the absence — of people who have been destroyed or disappeared.
The murdered Tulkinghorn, fresh in his mind. The vanished Lady Dedlock. The stricken Sir Leicester upstairs.
And the prose captures that state between fear and expectation — that Gothic moment where you almost want to see the ghost, and almost don't.
"He looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy."
"But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
That doubling of blank — it's scored for the voice. No actor needs to be told what to do with that.
The blank — and then the oppressive silence.
Dickens ends the passage with those words — and you feel the weight of all that emptiness.
But I want to come back to the question of what survives in this novel — because it isn't only darkness.
There's a passage spoken by Ada that I find almost too tender to read without a catch in the voice.
She's imagining a future for Richard — when she's old, or dead — when their child might somehow redeem what was ruined.
She says — and this is Ada's own voice, looking forward across years:
"Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the sunshine with him, honouring his grey head."
"And saying to himself, 'I thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me!'"
She doesn't know if Richard will survive long enough for any of this.
But she looks forward anyway. That's the whole shape of Ada's character — grief held inside hope.
What's remarkable about that speech is that Ada is imagining redemption through a generation that doesn't yet exist — a child not yet born.
It has the same structural quality as that Tulkinghorn passage — the future reaching back into the present.
But where the Tulkinghorn narration portends death, Ada's portends — or at least prays for — restoration.
The novel holds both at once. It won't let you settle.
And then there's Sir Leicester's declaration — which is the other great act of love in these later chapters.
He's been humiliated in the most public possible way. His wife's secret is out. He has had a stroke.
And what does he do? He gathers the household and formally declares his terms.
"I assert no cause whatever of complaint against her. That I have ever had the strongest affection for her, and that I retain it undiminished."
Undiminished. After everything. That word is doing enormous work.
Sir Leicester is a figure Dickens could easily have kept as a pompous target — and he is pompous, often.
But in these late chapters Dickens allows him genuine dignity. And that generosity is part of what makes the novel so large.
That word — undiminished — it lands differently once you know what has preceded it.
We have the comic satire of Kenge defending the indefensible, the gothic foreboding of the grave already being dug, the blank horror of George walking those empty rooms — and then this.
A man declaring love he will not revoke.
The architecture of this novel holds all of those registers simultaneously — and that, I think, is why it endures.
We'll be back after the break to look more closely at what the novel does with voice and narration.

segments.title: A World of Consequences: Synthesis and Reckoning

utterances.text: We've arrived at the close of today's episode, and I want to spend our final minutes doing what Dickens himself does so well — holding the threads together and feeling their full weight.
We've been circling Richard Carstone almost without naming him directly — and yet he haunts everything we've discussed today.
A young man who might have been anything, drifting toward ruin while everyone around him watches and worries.
Oliver, Caroline, James — I want each of you to take a moment of reckoning with what Dickens has shown us, and how.
What I keep returning to — and I suspect I always will — is that Dickens builds his doom in sunlight.
He doesn't reach for storm clouds or gothic machinery when he wants to signal catastrophe.
He gives you a burst of radiance and then he takes it away, quietly, without drama.
There's that passage where Esther watches Richard and Ada walk away through a sunlit room — and it is one of the most heartbreaking things in English fiction, and it looks like joy.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
That last line. The room darkened as they went out.
Dickens doesn't tell you Richard is doomed. He lets a cloud do it.
And what makes that passage almost unbearable is the line just before it — Esther watching Ada look up at Richard's face, listening, seeming to see nothing else.
Ada is entirely given over to him. Already. And we know where that leads.
What strikes me about the earlier scene — when they first confide in Esther and put her between them — is how much warmth Dickens allows.
He doesn't withhold affection from these young people. He adores them, even as he's setting the trap.
Esther says — and this is the counsel she offers them, quietly, steadily — that this love

"could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Constancy, fortitude, perseverance. Those are serious words for a tender scene.
Esther knows, even then, what it will cost them to be happy. She's telling us what Richard will fail to provide.
I want to come at Richard from a slightly different angle, because I think we risk making his failure purely psychological — a weakness of character, a personal flaw.
Dickens is more precise than that, and Mrs. Badger of all people makes the diagnosis exactly right.
Richard lacks what she calls — and I love that Dickens gives this to a minor comic character — he lacks a vocation.
Not ability. Not intelligence. A vocation — a positive interest — which is entirely different.
Mrs. Badger puts it plainly, and she is ruthlessly accurate, when she says of men like Woodcourt that they

"take it from a strong interest in all that it can do" and "will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
Work, endurance, disappointment. This is what commitment actually looks like. Not romance. Not promise.
Richard's tragedy is not simply that Chancery destroys him — it's that he never had the interior resources to resist it.
Jarndyce v Jarndyce doesn't corrupt a strong man. It finds an opening where there is already a vacancy.
A vacancy. That's exactly it. And Dickens is generous enough — or cruel enough — to show us the vacancy being formed before Chancery gets anywhere near him.
All those professions tried and discarded. All that restless energy with nowhere to go.
Richard will work his fingers to the bone for Ada — he says so himself, in that early scene, with complete sincerity.
The trouble is that sincerity, in Dickens, is never enough. You have to be able to sustain it across years and tedium and disappointment.
And the novel shows us, with terrible patience, that Richard cannot.
What moves me most, standing back from all of it, is Esther's position in these scenes.
She is placed between them — literally, physically, they pull chairs to either side of her.
And she watches them walk away into that clouded light, and she sees what's coming, and she can't stop it.
Esther is Dickens's moral centre in this novel — clear-sighted, loving, helpless.
That combination of seeing truly and being unable to prevent what you see — that's where the real tragedy lives.
And the institution — Chancery, the case — is what gives Richard's vacancy its particular shape and direction.
Without Jarndyce v Jarndyce, Richard might have drifted through life merely unfulfilled — restless but harmless.
The case gives the vacancy a purpose, a narrative, a reason to refuse all other purposes.
That is Dickens's indictment — not just of one young man's weakness, but of a system engineered to exploit it.
I think that's exactly where we should leave things — with that word, engineered.
A system that looks like justice and functions like a machine for consuming lives.
Richard and Ada walking into that burst of light — and then the cloud, and then the dark.
My deepest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done justice — real justice — to a very great novel.
Bleak House Unpacked will return. Until then, keep reading.

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.

bottle of light wine. Mr. Skimpole himself reclined upon the sofa in

words, for I happened afterwards to note them in my diary, which is
producible at any time—I mentioned to you that Mr. C. had laid down
the principle of watching his own interests, and that when a client
of mine laid down a principle which was not of an immoral (that is to
say, unlawful) nature, it devolved upon me to carry it out. I HAVE
carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over
to any connexion of Mr. C.’s on any account. As open as I was to Mr.
Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional
duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one. I openly say,
unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.’s affairs in a very
bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I

“Hush! Hush!” The housekeeper looks round and answers in a frightened
whisper, “My Lady, I have not breathed a word of it, I don’t believe
what’s written in it, I know it can’t be true, I am sure and certain
that it is not true. But my son is in danger, and you must have a
heart to pity me. If you know of anything that is not known to
others, if you have any suspicion, if you have any clue at all, and
any reason for keeping it in your own breast, oh, my dear Lady, think
of me, and conquer that reason, and let it be known! This is the most
I consider possible. I know you are not a hard lady, but you go your
own way always without help, and you are not familiar with your
friends; and all who admire you—and all do—as a beautiful and
elegant lady, know you to be one far away from themselves who can’t
be approached close. My Lady, you may have some proud or angry
reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,
oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been
passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with
genuine simplicity, “I am so humble in my place and you are by nature
so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child,
but I feel so much that I have come here to make so bold as to beg
and pray you not to be scornful of us if you can do us any right or

groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the

Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home...But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.

associated with the lonely days at my godmother’s; yes, away even to

I felt it to be an unmeaning weakness in me and tried to overcome it
by attending to the words I heard. Then, very strangely, I seemed to
hear them, not in the reader’s voice, but in the well-remembered
voice of my godmother. This made me think, did Lady Dedlock’s face
accidentally resemble my godmother’s? It might be that it did, a
little; but the expression was so different, and the stern decision
which had worn into my godmother’s face, like weather into rocks, was
so completely wanting in the face before me that it could not be that
resemblance which had struck me. Neither did I know the loftiness and
haughtiness of Lady Dedlock’s face, at all, in any one. And yet I—I,
little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on
whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own
eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady,
whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I
perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour.

This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with
something of a shadow on their benevolent expression. I well
remembered the look with which he had contemplated her and Richard

c23:p23.text:
At that time, and for a good many weeks after that time, Richard was
constant in his visits. Besides coming every Saturday or Sunday and
remaining with us until Monday morning, he sometimes rode out on
horseback unexpectedly and passed the evening with us and rode back
again early next day. He was as vivacious as ever and told us he was
very industrious, but I was not easy in my mind about him. It
appeared to me that his industry was all misdirected. I could not
find that it led to anything but the formation of delusive hopes in
connexion with the suit already the pernicious cause of so much
sorrow and ruin. He had got at the core of that mystery now, he told
us, and nothing could be plainer than that the will under which he
and Ada were to take I don’t know how many thousands of pounds must
be finally established if there were any sense or justice in the
Court of Chancery—but oh, what a great IF that sounded in my
ears—and that this happy conclusion could not be much longer
delayed. He proved this to himself by all the weary arguments on that
side he had read, and every one of them sunk him deeper in the
infatuation. He had even begun to haunt the court. He told us how he
saw Miss Flite there daily, how they talked together, and how he did
her little kindnesses, and how, while he laughed at her, he pitied
her from his heart. But he never thought—never, my poor, dear,
sanguine Richard, capable of so much happiness then, and with such
better things before him—what a fatal link was riveting between his
fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged
birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind.
c23:p23.summary: Esther describes Richard's constant visits and his growing fixation on Chancery, his delusional belief in an imminent favorable judgment, his friendship with Miss Flite, and her ominous premonition of the catastrophic effect this will have on him.
c23:p23.best_quote: Every one of them sunk him deeper in the infatuation...what a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind.

c12:p56.text:
Then there is my Lord Boodle, of considerable reputation with his
party, who has known what office is and who tells Sir Leicester
Dedlock with much gravity, after dinner, that he really does not see
to what the present age is tending. A debate is not what a debate
used to be; the House is not what the House used to be; even a
Cabinet is not what it formerly was. He perceives with astonishment
that supposing the present government to be overthrown, the limited
choice of the Crown, in the formation of a new ministry, would lie
between Lord Coodle and Sir Thomas Doodle—supposing it to be
impossible for the Duke of Foodle to act with Goodle, which may be
assumed to be the case in consequence of the breach arising out of
that affair with Hoodle. Then, giving the Home Department and the
leadership of the House of Commons to Joodle, the Exchequer to
Koodle, the Colonies to Loodle, and the Foreign Office to Moodle,
what are you to do with Noodle? You can’t offer him the Presidency of
the Council; that is reserved for Poodle. You can’t put him in the
Woods and Forests; that is hardly good enough for Quoodle. What
follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces
(as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock)
because you can’t provide for Noodle!
c12:p56.summary: Lord Boodle explains to Sir Leicester that government is failing because there is no office suitable for Noodle after all the important positions are distributed among his equally mediocre associates.
c12:p56.best_quote: What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!

c39:p4.text:
But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.
c39:p4.best_quote: Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth.

c41:p32.text:
Their need for watching one another should be over now, but they do
it all this time, and the stars watch them both through the opened
window. Away in the moonlight lie the woodland fields at rest, and
the wide house is as quiet as the narrow one. The narrow one! Where
are the digger and the spade, this peaceful night, destined to add
the last great secret to the many secrets of the Tulkinghorn
existence? Is the man born yet, is the spade wrought yet? Curious
questions to consider, more curious perhaps not to consider, under
the watching stars upon a summer night.
c41:p32.summary: The narrator reflects that the stars watch over Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock, then mysteriously asks about 'the digger and the spade' and the last great secret destined to be added to Tulkinghorn's existence.

c58:p98.text:
The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.
c58:p98.summary: George patrols the grand house, his memories of past and present mingling, sensing the shadows of the missing Lady Dedlock and the murdered Tulkinghorn, finding only emptiness.
c58:p98.best_quote: "he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below"

The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up
in his face, listening, and seemed to see nothing else. So young, so
beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through
the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the
years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed
away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that
had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun
was clouded over.

There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

“My dear Miss Summerson,” she replied, “on Mr. Carstone’s character
and conduct. He is of such a very easy disposition that probably he
would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels, but
he feels languid about the profession. He has not that positive
interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided
impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a
